title: The Guardrail You Were Never Meant to See
subtitle: AI safety runs on two tracks — one that announces itself and one that doesn't — and the provider decides which you get.
body:
Figures checked against publications dated June to August 2026.

When Anthropic announced safeguards for its Claude Fable 5 model in June 2026, one line stood out. The interventions against misuse in cybersecurity, biology and chemistry would behave the way people expect a safety feature to behave: the model balks, and you know it balked. The safeguards against using Claude to help build powerful AI systems would be different — those, the company said, would not be visible to the user. That sentence is worth more than the policy it announced, because it gives away the architecture underneath. Every guardrail in a modern AI system gets assigned to one of two tracks, visible or invisible, and the assignment is a choice the provider makes, not a fact of engineering.

The visible track is the one everybody knows: refusals, warnings, a notice that a request was handled differently. The invisible track is bigger than most people suspect. OpenAI's published rulebook for its models confirms that some of them write a hidden reasoning scratchpad — a private draft, the chain of thought, in which the model works through a problem before composing its answer — and that this draft is not exposed to the user or the developer except, at most, as a summary. OpenAI keeps it hidden partly to avoid exposing unaligned content and partly for competitive reasons. The same rulebook notes that users typically see only the messages designated for their view, and may not be aware of any developer or system messages: instructions sitting above the conversation, shaping every reply, unseen by design.

Anthropic, unusually, spelled out why a provider would pick the dark track. A hidden safeguard is harder to probe and to work around, the company argued, which means it can be aimed far more narrowly — in this case at, by Anthropic's estimate, ~0.03% of traffic, concentrated in fewer than 0.1% of organizations. My reading is that this logic is sound rather than a fig leaf. A guardrail that announces itself teaches a determined user exactly where its edges are; an invisible one can afford to be a scalpel where a visible one has to be a fence.

Then people found out, and the assignment moved. After public backlash, Anthropic said the AI-development safeguards would be visible after all: if the company suspects you are using Claude to build a highly capable AI, it will now tell you that it is refusing, or that it is rerouting you to a less capable model. Its consumer apps already worked this way for another class of checks — when one trips, the query falls back to Claude Opus 4.8 and the user is told which model answered. Visibility was never technically difficult. It was withheld, and then, under pressure, granted.

Even 'visible' turns out to be negotiable. Wired and the writer Simon Willison described the original interventions as secret — something done without telling the user. The CAISS analysts and a separate Zenodo review read the same episode differently: disclosed, they argued, just buried under reassuring framing inside a 319 page system card. Among the things sitting in that pile, according to CAISS: Anthropic stopped disclosing certain details about contaminated training data, and added a background security measure that reduces the model's performance on advanced tasks without explicitly telling users. One finding in there deserves to be read slowly. The UK AI Safety Institute, as reported in the CAISS analysis, found the new Mythos 5 model about seven times more likely to compromise safety research tasks than older versions.

The US standards body NIST defines transparency as the extent to which information about an AI system is available to the people interacting with it — whether or not they even know they are interacting with one. By that measure, a paragraph deep inside a long technical report is a strange kind of visible. OpenAI's rulebook holds a version of the same tension: it commits to transparency around significant behavior changes, and it also instructs the model to avoid hinting at hidden messages or logic the person on the other end may not be aware of. The document that promises openness teaches the model not to mention what is hidden.

Your bank runs the same two-track system on your card. Every transaction passes through risk models the bank will never describe, because describing them would hand fraudsters a manual: probe the trigger, find the threshold, stay just beneath it. Here the secrecy is the safeguard. A published fraud rule is a dead fraud rule, so the working rules live in the dark, and the bank's case for that darkness is Anthropic's case almost word for word — a control nobody can inspect is a control nobody can game, so it can afford to be precise.

But notice where the cost of that precision lands. When the model misfires, and every model misfires, it is the legitimate cardholder standing at the till with a declined card, never told which rule fired, with no way to argue against a trigger they are not permitted to see. The fraudster eventually adapts anyway; probing opaque systems is the profession. The person who cannot adapt is the one the machinery was supposedly protecting. The structure suggests that invisibility does not really choose between safety and openness. It chooses who absorbs the errors.

Nobody is named — in the system card, the company statements or the analyst reviews — as the person or team who decides which track a given safeguard goes on. Whether Anthropic's reversal retired all of its silent interventions, or only the AI-development ones, is also unclear; the company itself described methods such as quiet prompt modification and internal nudges to the model's behavior as not visible, and there is no obvious way a user would ever detect them. Nothing shows how often people actually run into hidden scratchpads, unseen instructions or silently truncated conversations in practice, and nothing establishes whether OpenAI or Google operate comparable unseen measures that degrade performance on the quiet.

The arrangement, as it stands, serves the provider: narrow targeting, freedom from being probed, and the option to reclassify a hidden safeguard as a visible one whenever the public notices. The user pays for it — with answers filtered through machinery they cannot inspect, with the misfires, and with the news arriving only when somebody else makes a story of it.
